subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Misinformation Effect: Rewriting Memory
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Misinformation Effect: Rewriting Memory.

hook.text: Elizabeth Loftus showed people a car crash video & asked 'How fast were the cars when they smashed?' Speed estimates.

buildup.text: The word 'smashed' instead of 'hit' changed what people remembered seeing — even adding broken glass that didn't exist.

discovery.text: Memory isn't a recording. It's a reconstruction — rebuilt every time you recall it, and vulnerable to new information.

twist.text: Leading questions can implant entirely false memories. Some subjects remembered events that never happened.

climax.text: This is why eyewitness testimony is unreliable — the Innocence Project overturned 375+ convictions based on it.

punchline.text: Your memory is confident. That doesn't make it accurate.

quiz.question: What did Elizabeth Loftus's car crash experiments demonstrate?
options: Subtle word changes can alter what people remember seeing
Memory is like a video recording

details.summary: The misinformation effect occurs when new information after an event distorts your memory of the original event. Leading questions, media coverage, and other people's accounts can literally rewrite what you remember.
details.whyItMatters: Eyewitness testimony, personal memories, and historical narratives are all vulnerable to post-event distortion, with serious consequences for justice and truth.
takeaways: Post-event information can alter existing memories
Leading questions reliably distort eyewitness recall
Elizabeth Loftus's research revolutionized understanding of memory

faq.question: How did Elizabeth Loftus demonstrate the misinformation effect?
faq.answer: Loftus showed participants a car crash video, then asked some about the cars 'smashing' and others about cars 'hitting.' The 'smashing' group remembered the crash as faster and even recalled broken glass that was never there.

faq.question: What are the real-world consequences of the misinformation effect?
faq.answer: Wrongful convictions based on distorted eyewitness testimony are the most serious consequence. The Innocence Project found that mistaken eyewitness identification contributed to over 70% of overturned convictions.
